candidates.attacker_control: JiffleRIF.create reads the `script` and `sourceNames` parameters from the JAI ParameterBlock, and JiffleDescriptor.create exposes both as operation parameters. Jiffle.setScript/setImageParams and JiffleBuilder.source/dest also accept caller strings. In a deployed service, the attack path is a user who can submit a Jiffle script, for example through a Jiffle WPS process or rendering transformation, or who can control source image variable names.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I checked for sanitization: stripComments removes only `/* ... */` block comments, not `//` line comments; Jiffle.setImageParams and VarWorker.addImageVarsToGlobal perform no Java-identifier validation; JiffleRIF checks only array lengths, not content. The scriptInDocs flag does not mitigate because createRuntimeSource always calls writer.setScript(stripComments(theScript)), and the code even throws when scriptInDocs is true. JiffleRIF uses the INDIRECT model, so destination-name fields are skipped, but source names are emitted for both models. Jiffle being a compiled scripting language is expected; the issue is the unescaped escape from the DSL into generated Java. No sandbox or security manager is configured around Janino.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary Java code execution in the application/JVM context, potentially leading to full server compromise, data disclosure or tampering, and denial of service. Malformed script/name text can also force compilation failures and deny Jiffle processing.
candidates.prerequisites: Ability to supply a Jiffle script and/or source image names to a Jiffle execution path. For the script-in-Javadoc variant, the Jiffle lexer must accept `//` line comments; the language does, but the ANTLR grammar is absent from this snapshot to verify directly. Janino uses its default compiler/classloader, with no restricted classes or SecurityManager. The injected text must produce a compilable class or execute when the generated runtime class is initialized.
candidates.root_cause: Jiffle translates scripts to Java source by string concatenation. Script.write embeds raw script lines inside a `/** ... */` Javadoc block, and emits image variable names directly as Java identifiers and string literals. Jiffle.createRuntimeSource applies only a block-comment stripper and always includes the script even though the runtime-instance path passes `scriptInDocs=false`. JiffleRIF and Jiffle.setImageParams accept caller-supplied image names with no Java-identifier validation. The resulting source is compiled by org.codehaus.janino.SimpleCompiler and instantiated without a sandbox.
candidates.title: Java code injection in Jiffle-generated runtime source
candidates.trace: JiffleRIF.create -> getRuntime -> Jiffle.setScript/setImageParams -> Jiffle.compile (parse/AST) -> getRuntimeInstance -> createRuntimeSource -> writer.setScript(stripComments(theScript)) -> Script.write (raw script inside `/** ... */`, plus `s_<name>`/`d_<name>` fields and `_images.get("<name>")` literals) -> SimpleCompiler.cook -> loadClass(...).newInstance(). A `//` comment containing a Javadoc terminator survives stripComments and closes the generated comment; a name containing Java syntax breaks out of the field/string context. The injected Java is compiled and run in-process.
candidates.unverified: The Jiffle ANTLR grammar (.g4) is absent from the snapshot, so the `//` line-comment variant is inferred from the language and the block-comment-only stripper rather than confirmed. No runtime execution or exploit was performed. I could not verify that a real deployment exposes sourceNames to untrusted users; the script path is the more clearly exposed one. Whether Janino accepts the exact injected class/initializer structure was not tested.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

coverage_summary: All 490 model-visible files were enumerated across the listed modules. The Jiffle language/compiler/operator paths were read in depth, and all files were searched for process execution, script engines, dynamic compilation, deserialization, XML parsing, file/network I/O, reflection/classloading, regex, and dynamic array allocation. Large numeric image-operation files were spot-checked and searched rather than read line-by-line.
limitations: No tests, packaged resources, or the Jiffle ANTLR .g4 grammar are present in the snapshot; comment syntax and build-time behavior could not be verified.
No external GeoServer/Jiffle integration source is in this repository, so remote reachability of the script/sourceNames parameters is not proven.
No code was executed and no runtime confirmation was attempted.
Several large numeric operation files (hundreds of KB each) were not fully line-by-line reviewed.

rejected_leads.lead: Destination image name injection through JiffleRIF/SetDestValue
rejected_leads.reason: JiffleRIF uses the INDIRECT runtime model, and Script.write emits destination fields only for DIRECT mode; the destination name would also need a corresponding script reference. Not selected as a separate candidate.
OptionsBlockWorker/OptionInfo accept only numeric values, `null`, or known constants and re-serialize those values; OptionLookup substitutes only validated values. No source injection path found.

rejected_leads.lead: Arbitrary Java through Jiffle function names
rejected_leads.reason: FunctionLookup restricts names to the classpath FunctionLookup.properties file, unknown functions are reported as errors, and runtime expressions come from trusted properties. Not a caller-controlled sink.

The parser loads class names from registry resources discovered on the classpath. An attacker able to modify that resource or add a malicious JAR already controls the classpath, so this is not a distinct remote vulnerability.

Broad searches and spot checks of the large numeric operation files found Java array accesses that fail with exceptions rather than memory corruption; no strong attacker-controlled source-to-sink path was established. Possible denial of service was not selected over the Jiffle code-injection lead.
The explicit file reads are in demo applications or the image viewer and are not part of a server-side untrusted-input path in this snapshot.

summary: Reviewed the 490-file JAI-EXT source snapshot, with deep inspection of the Jiffle script compiler/operator and broad searches for process execution, dynamic compilation, deserialization, XML, file/network I/O, reflection, and array/loop patterns. The strongest lead is Java source injection in Jiffle runtime generation: raw script text and image variable names are concatenated into generated Java source, then compiled and instantiated by Janino. This can turn a Jiffle script or source-name parameter into arbitrary Java code execution. No candidate was runtime-confirmed.
